 AI-powered weather forecasting system seen boosting agri, flood prediction 
 A NEW artificial intelligence (AI)-powered weather forecasting system is expected to help mitigate Philippine agriculture’s vulnerability to weather events while improving flood warnings, the Department of Science and Technology said. 
 November 17, 2026 | 8:41 pm 
 ATMO.AI 
 By Beatriz Marie D. Cruz, Senior Reporter 
 A NEW arti fi cial intelligence (AI)-powered weather forecasting system is expected to help mitigate Philippine agriculture’s vulnerability to weather events while improving fl ood warnings, the Department of Science and Technology said.
 “This AI technology offers immense promise to protect agricultural yields, sharpen early flood warnings, landslide warnings, and strengthen community resilience against severe climate events,” Science and Technology Secretary Renato U. Solidum, Jr. said on Tuesday during the system’s launch. 
 Atmo Chief Executive Of fi cer Alexander Levy said the new system promises to help mitigate vulnerabilities to the worsening dry spells, including threats to agriculture and health.
 “As the super El Niño approaches, it’s fortunate that the new national AI forecast is among the best at forecasting dangerous weather events,” Mr. Levy said in a statement.
 Over a hundred cities and municipalities have been placed under a State of Calamity due to the El Niño, which is currently active and expected to peak in early 2027.
 The Philippines is one of the most vulnerable countries to calamities in the world, with about 20 typhoons traversing its territory annually.
 The AI weather forecasting system is now integrated with the nationwide network of Doppler radars, surface stations and satellite feeds operated by the government weather service, known as PAGASA (Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration). 
 The new AI-driven weather forecast system promises to predict atmospheric conditions with up to 100 times more geographic detail   and up to 14 days in advance.
 It can also issue weather assessments every 15 minutes, compared to the old system’s three-hour interval.
 “The forecast was also independently evaluated by Scripps over a year of real data and found to be most accurate for predicting impactful weather events such as heavy rain, typhoons and heat waves,” Atmo said, referring to a University of California institute conducting earth science research. 
 The AI   has been trained and tailored to assess data specific to the Philippines, Atmo said.
 Mr. Solidum said using AI to improve climate resilience should be adopted region-wide. 
 “Climate risks are shared challenges, and the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) member states must navigate this technological frontier together under shared ethical standards, interoperable data frameworks, and mutual trust,” he said.
